# Quick start
- 1. Tap “Add a lamp”.
- 2. Pick how to connect (see below).
- 3. Tap Blink to test. Keep the connections that make the lamp flash, then Save.
- 4. Tap your lamp to control it.

# Three ways to add a lamp
- Copy from a remote: press a button on the lamp's own remote while the app listens. Also works with the lamp's app on another phone. Nothing is changed on the lamp.
- Paste a captured packet: for advanced users who captured the lamp's signal.
- Pair as a new remote: power-cycle the lamp, then press Pair. Best choice if you only have your phone.

# Controlling a lamp
- ON / OFF switch the light.
- Brightness and color temperature are sent when you let go of the slider.
- Auto-off timer: the lamp turns itself off after 1–10 minutes.
- The lamp never reports its state, so the app remembers the last command it sent.

# Widgets and shortcuts
- Long-press your home screen, choose Widgets, then find this app. The ★ lamp is the one the widgets control.
- Inside a lamp you can add an ON / OFF shortcut or timer shortcuts to your home screen.

# If the lamp does not react
- Stand close to the lamp.
- Open the lamp, tap Edit & test, then Blink on each connection.
- Close the lamp's original app: it can interfere.
- Power-cycle the lamp and pair again.
- Keep Bluetooth switched on.

# How these lamps work
- These lamps have no Wi-Fi and no normal Bluetooth connection.
- A remote (or app) shouts short Bluetooth broadcasts. The lamp obeys only the broadcasts that carry an ID it has memorised.
- That is why a lamp ignores a new remote until it has been paired.

# Pairing
- Pairing simply teaches the lamp a new ID.
- For a few seconds after power-up, most lamps accept a new ID. The remote then sends a “pair” message that contains its ID.
- Most lamps remember several remotes, so pairing this app normally keeps your old remote working. A few lamps forget the oldest one.
- The lamp gives no feedback. That is why this app has the Blink test.

# Copying instead of pairing
- If the app can hear your existing remote, it copies that remote's ID. Both keep working and you never have to pair.

# Why several connections?
- Many lamp apps broadcast two protocol versions at once (for example V1 and V2). The app keeps every version that works.

# Resetting a lamp
- Cutting the power and pairing a new remote is how lamps are re-assigned. Some physical remotes also have a pair / unpair button.

# BLE ADV for Humans
- A simple remote for Bluetooth-broadcast lamps such as LampSmart Pro.
- It builds on the open source protocol work of the ha-ble-adv project and makes it friendly for everyone.

# How sure are we?
- Tested on a real lamp: LampSmart Pro (the author's lamp).
- Every other brand below is verified against the test data of the open source ha-ble-adv project (hundreds of packets match byte for byte), but has NOT been tried on real lamps by the author. If you have one, please tell us how it went (see About).

# Brands you can pair with this app
- LampSmart Pro and FanLamp Pro (also seen in apps such as ApplianceSmart and Vmax smart)
- Zhi Jia, Zhi Guang, Zhi Guang 2
- Zhi Mei Deng Kong (light and fan versions)
- Smart Light (Agarce)
- LE Light
- RuiXin
- RW.LIGHT
- Smart Elfin

# Brands you can add by copying a remote
- Mantra, Dudugu, HxLight / LED-Spots and eWeLink (only the devices that use Bluetooth advertising) have no working pairing step in the reference project. Copy the signal of their remote, or paste a captured packet.

# What the app can control
- Lights: on / off, brightness and color temperature, RGB colors (where the protocol has them), a second light, auto-off timer (where the lamp supports it).
- Fans: the protocols are included and verified, but fan controls are not in the app screens yet.

# Limits
- Two FanLamp remote types (r0, r1) can only be listened to, not controlled.
- One Zhi Mei fan remote format uses raw radio bytes that Android cannot broadcast.
- Lamps that use RF (433 MHz) or infrared remotes, or a normal Bluetooth connection (GATT), are not supported.
- Android controls the small “flags” byte of the broadcast. The reference decoder ignores it, and the tested lamp works without it.
